title: Diseases of Endocrine Hypofunction
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers diseases in which a gland makes too little hormone or its target cannot respond: diabetes insipidus, primary, acute, and secondary adrenal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathyroidism, hypopituitarism and hypothalamic lesions, the hypothyroid states, nonthyroidal illness, and short stature. Each axis is a feedback loop, so pairing the trophic hormone with its target hormone locates the defect: a low target hormone with a high trophic hormone means the gland or end organ has failed, while a low target hormone with a low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone means the pituitary or hypothalamus has failed. The electrolyte, skin, and cardiovascular findings then follow from what each missing hormone normally does.
prerequisites: Hypothalamic and pituitary anatomy, the hypophyseal portal circulation, and negative feedback (EN-3, EN-5, EN-6)
ADH action on the collecting duct and the medullary concentrating gradient
Adrenal cortical zones, their hormones, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
PTH, calcitriol, and calcium and phosphate handling by bone, gut, and kidney (EN-5)
Thyroid hormone synthesis, deiodination, and nuclear receptor action (EN-8)

connections.how: Each hypofunction state here has a mirror-image excess state, and the same trophic and target hormone pairing locates both.
Diabetes insipidus, aldosterone deficiency, and PTH deficiency are read through water, potassium, hydrogen ion, calcium, and phosphate handling by the nephron.
Hyperkalemia from aldosterone loss and the long QT of hypocalcemia are electrolyte effects on the cardiac action potential.
Autoimmune adrenalitis, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, tuberculosis, and meningococcemia are leading causes of gland destruction.
DiGeorge syndrome, thyroid dysgenesis, GNAS imprinting, and X-linked V2 receptor defects explain congenital forms.

terms.def: Failure of the target gland itself, so its hormone is low and the pituitary trophic hormone rises.
Failure of the pituitary to secrete a trophic hormone, so both trophic and target hormones are low; failure of the hypothalamus is sometimes called tertiary.
Failure of target tissue to respond to a hormone that is present, so hormone levels rise while the clinical picture resembles deficiency.
Excretion of large volumes of dilute urine because ADH is absent (central) or the kidney cannot respond to it (nephrogenic).
A synthetic ADH analog selective for the V2 receptor, used in testing to ask whether the collecting duct can respond to ADH.
The precursor protein cleaved in corticotrophs to ACTH and related peptides, including melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).
Acute, life-threatening cortisol deficiency, with or without aldosterone deficiency, presenting as shock.
Involuntary sustained muscle contraction caused by spontaneous firing of hyperexcitable motor nerves, as in hypocalcemia.
A phenotype of short stature, round face, obesity, and short fourth and fifth metacarpals caused by inactivating GNAS mutations.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland, from any cause, most often TSH-driven hyperplasia when hormone synthesis is impaired.
An inactive isomer of T3 formed when type 3 deiodinase removes an iodine from the inner ring of T4.
Skeletal maturity judged from a hand and wrist radiograph and compared with chronological age.

blocks.text: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, carried down axons in the pituitary stalk, and released from the posterior pituitary. Osmoreceptors trigger release when plasma osmolality rises by as little as about 1%; a large fall in blood volume or pressure is a second, less sensitive stimulus. ADH binds V2 receptors on principal cells of the collecting duct. The Gs-cAMP-protein kinase A pathway inserts aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, and water leaves through basolateral aquaporin-3 and aquaporin-4 into the hypertonic medulla. ADH also raises urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct, which helps maintain the medullary gradient.

blocks.title: From ADH release to concentrated urine
steps: Rising plasma osmolality stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors
ADH released from posterior pituitary
ADH binds V2 receptor on principal cell
Gs raises cAMP, protein kinase A activated
Aquaporin-2 inserted into apical membrane
Water moves into hypertonic medulla, urine concentrated
blocks.caption: Central diabetes insipidus breaks the chain at ADH release; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus breaks it at the V2 receptor, cAMP signaling, or aquaporin-2.

blocks.text: Diabetes insipidus is the loss of this system. In central diabetes insipidus too little ADH is secreted. Symptoms usually appear only after most of the ADH-producing neurons are lost, and lesions low on the stalk spare more function than lesions near the hypothalamus because ADH can still be released from the cut proximal end. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus ADH is present, often raised, but the collecting duct cannot respond.

blocks.title: Causes of diabetes insipidus
rows: Head trauma, pituitary or hypothalamic surgery
Damage to ADH neurons or their axons in the stalk
Craniopharyngioma, germinoma, metastases, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoidosis
Destruction or infiltration of the hypothalamus or stalk
Inflammation of hypothalamic nuclei or the stalk
Enters principal cells through ENaC and reduces aquaporin-2 expression
Calcium-sensing receptor activation reduces aquaporin-2 and weakens the medullary gradient
Reduced aquaporin-2 expression and a weaker medullary gradient
blocks.caption: Central causes act on ADH supply; nephrogenic causes act on the collecting duct response.

blocks.text: Both forms produce the same picture: polyuria (more than about 3 L per day in an adult), nocturia, intense thirst, and inappropriately dilute urine, usually below about 300 mOsm/kg and often below 200 mOsm/kg in complete disease. Thirst normally replaces the lost water, so serum sodium stays high-normal. Hypernatremia (sodium above about 145 mEq/L) appears when intake cannot keep up: in infants, in elderly or obtunded patients, after surgery, or when a hypothalamic lesion also destroys the thirst center. This separates diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia, in which excess drinking comes first and plasma sodium and osmolality run low-normal.

The water deprivation test asks two questions in sequence. First, when the patient is dehydrated, can the body concentrate urine with its own ADH? Second, if it cannot, does the kidney respond when ADH activity is supplied as desmopressin? Fluids are withheld while urine osmolality, plasma osmolality or sodium, and body weight are measured at intervals. Deprivation ends when urine osmolality plateaus, plasma osmolality or sodium rises above normal, or body weight falls by about 3 to 5%. Desmopressin is then given and urine osmolality is measured again.

A healthy person concentrates urine well above plasma during deprivation, often to more than about 600 to 800 mOsm/kg, because rising osmolality releases endogenous ADH; desmopressin then adds little, since ADH is already acting at full effect. In central diabetes insipidus the dehydrated patient cannot release ADH, so urine stays dilute, but the collecting duct is intact and urine osmolality rises sharply (commonly by more than about 50%) after desmopressin. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus urine stays dilute both before and after desmopressin, because the defect lies beyond ADH. Primary polydipsia behaves like the normal response, although the maximum concentration may be somewhat reduced because chronic water loading washes out solute from the medullary interstitium.

blocks.title: Expected results of water deprivation and desmopressin
blocks.caption: Deprivation tests endogenous ADH release; desmopressin tests the kidney's response to ADH.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the two steps
blocks.text: A man with polyuria has a plasma sodium of 144 mEq/L. After 6 hours of water deprivation his plasma osmolality is 302 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality is 180 mOsm/kg. Step 1: plasma is concentrated, yet urine is less concentrated than plasma, so ADH is either missing or ineffective; primary polydipsia is excluded. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 520 mOsm/kg, nearly a threefold increase. Step 2: the collecting duct responds to ADH, so the receptor and aquaporin-2 pathway work and the defect is ADH supply. This is central diabetes insipidus. If urine had stayed near 200 mOsm/kg, the lesion would be nephrogenic.

Primary adrenal insufficiency is destruction of the adrenal cortex itself, so all three zones fail together: the zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), the zona fasciculata (cortisol), and the zona reticularis (adrenal androgens). Symptoms usually appear only after about 90% of both cortices are destroyed, which explains why the onset is gradual and why unilateral disease does not cause it. In developed countries the most common cause is autoimmune adrenalitis, with lymphocytic infiltration and autoantibodies most often directed against 21-hydroxylase; it may be isolated or part of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (AIRE mutation, with hypoparathyroidism and mucocutaneous candidiasis) or type 2 (with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes). Worldwide, tuberculosis is a leading cause, through caseating destruction that may later calcify. Bilateral metastases, most often from lung or breast carcinoma, and disseminated fungal infection are other causes.

blocks.title: Feedback in primary adrenal failure
steps: Adrenal cortex destroyed, cortisol falls
Less negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary
CRH and POMC synthesis increase
ACTH and MSH rise but cannot restore cortisol
blocks.caption: The loop stays open: rising ACTH cannot act on a destroyed cortex, so ACTH remains high.

blocks.text: Each finding follows from a missing hormone. Aldosterone normally drives sodium reabsorption through ENaC in principal cells, with potassium secretion through ROMK and hydrogen ion secretion by intercalated cells. Without it the kidney wastes sodium and water, plasma volume falls, and potassium and hydrogen ion are retained, giving hypotension, salt craving, hyperkalemia, and a mild non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Renin rises because volume is low. Hyponatremia has two sources: renal sodium loss, and increased ADH release from both hypovolemia and cortisol deficiency, since cortisol normally restrains ADH and is needed to excrete free water.

Cortisol loss causes fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, fasting hypoglycemia (less gluconeogenesis), and eosinophilia and lymphocytosis. Low cortisol removes feedback, so the pituitary increases POMC synthesis. Cleavage of POMC yields ACTH and related melanocortin peptides including MSH, and ACTH itself also stimulates the melanocortin 1 receptor on melanocytes, increasing melanin. Hyperpigmentation therefore appears in sun-exposed skin, palmar creases, knuckles, scars, gums, and buccal mucosa. Loss of adrenal androgens reduces axillary and pubic hair in women, who depend on adrenal precursors for much of their androgen.

Adrenal crisis is an acute shortfall of cortisol relative to need. A normal adrenal can increase cortisol output several-fold during infection, surgery, or trauma. A patient whose adrenal or pituitary reserve is lost cannot, so a stress that a healthy person tolerates becomes life-threatening. Three settings account for most cases.

blocks.title: Causes of adrenal crisis
rows: Stress (infection, surgery, trauma, vomiting) in known chronic insufficiency
Demand rises but cortisol cannot increase
Low in primary disease, preserved in secondary
Suppressed CRH and ACTH and an atrophied fasciculata cannot restart quickly
Preserved, because the glomerulosa does not depend on ACTH
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage: anticoagulation, DIC, antiphospholipid syndrome
Hemorrhagic adrenal necrosis in fulminant sepsis, classically Neisseria meningitidis, with DIC
blocks.caption: Infection is the most common trigger in known insufficiency; hemorrhage is the most abrupt cause.

blocks.text: The adrenal is vulnerable to hemorrhage because it has a rich arterial supply draining into a single central vein. Venous congestion or thrombosis, or a coagulopathy, therefore causes hemorrhage into the gland. In meningococcemia, endotoxin-driven DIC and endothelial injury produce bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis together with a purpuric rash.

Shock is the central feature, and cortisol explains why. Cortisol is permissive for vascular tone: it maintains expression of adrenergic receptors and the vascular response to catecholamines and angiotensin II, and it supports endothelial integrity. Cortisol delivered through the intra-adrenal portal blood also induces phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase in the medulla, so epinephrine synthesis falls with it. Without cortisol, vessels dilate and respond poorly to catecholamines, producing hypotension that responds poorly to fluids and vasopressors. In primary disease, aldosterone loss adds volume depletion and hyperkalemia. Patients also have abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, confusion, hypoglycemia, and hyponatremia, which can mimic an acute abdomen or sepsis.

blocks.title: From cortisol loss to shock
steps: Stress raises cortisol demand
Adrenal or pituitary cannot increase cortisol
Vessels lose adrenergic responsiveness and tone
Aldosterone loss adds sodium and water depletion (primary)
Vasodilation and hypovolemia lower blood pressure
Shock unresponsive to fluids and pressors alone
blocks.caption: The aldosterone step applies only when the cortex itself has failed.

blocks.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency is cortisol deficiency caused by too little ACTH. The most common cause overall is suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis by long-term exogenous glucocorticoids, which feed back on CRH and ACTH just as cortisol does. Pituitary causes include macroadenoma, surgery, radiation, Sheehan necrosis, and apoplexy, often with other pituitary deficits. Hypothalamic disease that removes CRH (tertiary insufficiency) behaves the same way.

Two classic signs of primary disease are absent, and both are predictable. ACTH is low, so there is no excess POMC-derived peptide and no hyperpigmentation; patients may look pale. Aldosterone is regulated mainly by angiotensin II and plasma potassium, with ACTH only a minor, short-term influence, so the zona glomerulosa keeps working. Potassium therefore stays normal, salt craving and severe volume depletion are uncommon, and renin is not markedly raised.

Cortisol deficiency still causes fatigue, weight loss, hypoglycemia, and hyponatremia. The hyponatremia here is dilutional rather than salt-losing: cortisol deficiency increases ADH release and impairs free water excretion, so water is retained while volume is near normal. Chronic ACTH deficiency also causes the fasciculata and reticularis to atrophy. This is why the adrenal response to an ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test is blunted in long-standing secondary disease even though the gland is not destroyed, but may still be normal soon after a sudden pituitary insult.

blocks.title: Primary versus secondary adrenal insufficiency
rows: Often deficient if the pituitary is diseased
blocks.caption: ACTH level and the presence of hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation separate the two forms.

blocks.predict: A patient stops prednisone abruptly after a year of high-dose use. Predict the ACTH, aldosterone, potassium, and skin findings.
blocks.explain: ACTH is suppressed, so cortisol falls without hyperpigmentation; angiotensin II still drives aldosterone, so potassium stays normal.
blocks.check: Compare with the primary versus secondary table and the regulation of the zona glomerulosa.

blocks.text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is secreted when the calcium-sensing receptor on chief cells detects a fall in ionized calcium. It raises calcium and lowers phosphate by three actions: it increases calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, inhibits sodium-phosphate cotransport in the proximal tubule, and stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase so that calcitriol increases intestinal absorption. It also mobilizes calcium from bone. In hypoparathyroidism all of these fail together, giving low serum calcium, high phosphate, low calcitriol, and a PTH that is low or inappropriately normal for the calcium level.

blocks.title: Causes of hypoparathyroidism
rows: Surgical removal or devascularization during thyroid, parathyroid, or neck surgery
Most common cause; may be transient or permanent
Autoimmune, isolated or in autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1
Immune destruction of chief cells; APS-1 adds Addison disease and candidiasis
Failure of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches: no parathyroids and thymic hypoplasia with T cell deficiency
Magnesium is needed for PTH secretion and action, so PTH is low and less effective
Chief cells sense normal calcium as high and suppress PTH
blocks.caption: Low PTH with low calcium and high phosphate defines true hypoparathyroidism whatever the cause.

blocks.text: The neuromuscular signs come from the effect of extracellular calcium on voltage-gated sodium channels. Calcium ions bound to the outer membrane surface raise the threshold for channel opening. When ionized calcium falls, sodium channels open at a less depolarized voltage, so peripheral nerves fire spontaneously and repetitively. Sensory nerves give perioral and fingertip numbness and tingling; motor nerves give cramps, carpopedal spasm, and in severe cases laryngospasm and seizures. Alkalosis worsens symptoms because albumin binds more calcium and ionized calcium falls, which is why hyperventilation can provoke tetany.

items: Chvostek sign: tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear causes twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles; it is also seen in some healthy people.

Trousseau sign: inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for about 3 minutes causes carpal spasm (wrist and metacarpophalangeal flexion, interphalangeal extension, thumb adduction); it is more specific.

blocks.text: In the heart, hypocalcemia lengthens the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential, which prolongs the ST segment and therefore the QT interval, while the T wave itself is usually normal. Chronic hypoparathyroidism also causes basal ganglia calcification, cataracts, and dental abnormalities if it begins in childhood. Total calcium must be read with albumin, since low albumin lowers total calcium without changing ionized calcium; a common correction adds 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL. Normal total calcium is about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L) and phosphate about 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism is end-organ resistance to PTH. The PTH receptor (PTH1R) signals through the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit (Gs alpha), which activates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP. Gs alpha is encoded by GNAS, an imprinted gene. In the renal proximal tubule and in some endocrine tissues (thyroid, gonads, pituitary somatotrophs), Gs alpha is expressed mainly from the maternal allele, while most other tissues express both alleles. This tissue-specific imprinting explains the inheritance pattern.

In pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a, an inactivating GNAS mutation inherited from the mother removes nearly all Gs alpha in the proximal tubule. The kidney cannot respond to PTH: phosphate is retained and calcitriol is not made. Serum calcium falls and phosphate rises, exactly as in true hypoparathyroidism, but the parathyroid glands are healthy and respond to hypocalcemia, so PTH is high. Because one functional allele is missing in all tissues, patients also have Albright hereditary osteodystrophy: short stature, round face, obesity, subcutaneous ossification, and brachydactyly with short fourth and fifth metacarpals. Resistance to other Gs-coupled hormones, especially TSH and gonadotropins, is common. In the classic test, giving PTH fails to raise urinary cAMP, which places the block before cAMP formation.

When the same mutation is inherited from the father, the kidney still expresses Gs alpha from the normal maternal allele, so PTH acts normally and calcium is normal. The patient has the Albright phenotype without hormone resistance, called pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. Type 1b results from defective methylation of the GNAS locus and causes renal PTH resistance without the Albright phenotype.

blocks.title: Distinguishing low calcium states by PTH
blocks.caption: High phosphate with low calcium points to PTH deficiency or resistance; PTH level separates the two. Low phosphate points to vitamin D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism.

blocks.predict: Two unrelated children both have short fourth metacarpals from an inactivating GNAS mutation. One has tetany and the other has normal calcium. Predict which parent passed the mutation to each child.
blocks.explain: The child with tetany inherited it from the mother, because the renal tubule expresses Gs alpha mainly from the maternal allele; the child with normal calcium inherited it from the father.
blocks.check: Compare with the imprinting paragraph and the table.

blocks.text: Hypopituitarism is deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones. Clinical deficiency usually appears only after about 75% of the anterior lobe is lost. When loss is gradual, as with compression, GH and the gonadotropins usually fail first, then TSH, and ACTH last, while prolactin is typically preserved or even mildly raised. ACTH loss is the most dangerous deficit because it can cause adrenal crisis. The posterior pituitary usually keeps working in pituitary adenoma, so diabetes insipidus suggests a hypothalamic or stalk lesion instead.

blocks.title: Major causes of hypopituitarism
rows: Compression of normal pituitary and stalk
Headache, bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression
Pregnancy enlarges the gland by lactotroph hyperplasia without matching blood supply; postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension cause infarction
Failure to lactate, then amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency
Sudden hemorrhage or infarction, usually into an adenoma
Sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia from cavernous sinus nerve compression, adrenal crisis
Removal or damage of normal tissue or stalk
Delayed damage to pituitary and hypothalamus
Deficits develop over years; GH is most sensitive
Hypophysitis often occurs in late pregnancy or postpartum
blocks.caption: Sheehan necrosis and apoplexy are acute and vascular; adenoma and radiation are gradual.

blocks.text: Each deficit has a predictable picture. GH deficiency causes poor growth in children and reduced lean mass and increased fat in adults. Gonadotropin deficiency causes amenorrhea, infertility, low libido, and loss of secondary sexual characteristics. TSH deficiency causes central hypothyroidism, and ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency without hyperpigmentation or hyperkalemia. In each case the target hormone is low and the trophic hormone is low or inappropriately normal.

The diaphragma sellae is a fold of dura that roofs the sella turcica and is pierced only by the pituitary stalk. In primary empty sella syndrome this diaphragm is congenitally incomplete, so the arachnoid and its CSF-filled subarachnoid space herniate into the sella. CSF pulsation flattens the pituitary against the floor, and imaging shows a sella that appears empty. It is common in obese, multiparous women and in idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Pituitary function is usually normal because the flattened tissue still works, although mild hyperprolactinemia from stalk traction or hypopituitarism can occur. Secondary empty sella follows loss of pituitary tissue from surgery, radiation, apoplexy, or Sheehan necrosis.

The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary through releasing hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) secreted into the hypophyseal portal veins at the median eminence. Prolactin is the exception: it is under tonic inhibition by dopamine delivered through the same portal veins. ADH is made by hypothalamic neurons and travels down the stalk to the posterior pituitary. A lesion of the hypothalamus or upper stalk therefore produces three linked findings, which together identify the site.

blocks.title: Predicting the effects of a hypothalamic or stalk lesion
steps: Lesion destroys hypothalamic nuclei or upper stalk
Releasing hormones fail to reach the anterior pituitary
GH, LH, FSH, TSH, and ACTH fall
Dopamine delivery fails, so prolactin rises
ADH neurons damaged, causing central diabetes insipidus
blocks.caption: Low anterior pituitary output with high prolactin and diabetes insipidus points above the pituitary.

blocks.text: Prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone that rises, and usually only mildly, a pattern called the stalk effect. A small or modest prolactin rise with a large sellar mass therefore suggests stalk compression rather than a prolactinoma. Diabetes insipidus is common because the lesion reaches ADH neurons or their axons above the median eminence. It may be masked when ACTH deficiency coexists, since cortisol is needed to excrete free water, and appear once cortisol is restored.

blocks.title: Causes of hypothalamic dysfunction
rows: Arises from Rathke pouch remnants; peaks in children and older adults; suprasellar, cystic, often calcified, with oily fluid; growth failure, bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes insipidus
Granulomas or histiocytes in the hypothalamus and stalk; diabetes insipidus is a classic presentation
Suprasellar germ cell tumor in children and young adults, often with diabetes insipidus
Delayed loss of releasing hormones; GH deficiency first
Shearing of the stalk or hypothalamus
blocks.caption: Diabetes insipidus at presentation favors a hypothalamic or stalk lesion over a pituitary adenoma.

blocks.text: Because the hypothalamus also controls appetite, temperature, thirst, and sleep, large lesions add hyperphagia and obesity, temperature instability, somnolence, and loss of thirst. Loss of thirst with diabetes insipidus is especially dangerous because water loss is not replaced and severe hypernatremia develops.

blocks.predict: A child with a calcified suprasellar mass has polyuria, slowed growth, and a mildly raised prolactin. Explain why prolactin rose while GH fell.
blocks.explain: The lesion stops both GHRH and dopamine reaching the pituitary; loss of a stimulator lowers GH, while loss of the inhibitor releases prolactin.
blocks.check: Compare with the flow figure and the stalk effect paragraph.

sections.title: Iodine deficiency goiter and the manifestations of hypothyroidism

blocks.text: Iodide is concentrated into follicular cells by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), oxidized and attached to tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase, and coupled to form T4 and T3. Adults need about 150 micrograms of iodine per day, more in pregnancy. When supply falls, less hormone is made. The gland adapts by trapping iodide more avidly and by making relatively more T3, which needs one fewer iodine atom and is more potent, but output still falls and the pituitary responds.

blocks.title: From iodine deficiency to multinodular goiter
steps: Dietary iodine deficient
Less T4 and T3 synthesized
Less negative feedback, TSH rises
Follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia: diffuse goiter
Repeated cycles of hyperplasia and involution
Uneven follicle growth, hemorrhage, fibrosis: multinodular goiter
blocks.caption: TSH drives growth; over years, heterogeneous follicle clones turn diffuse enlargement into nodules.

blocks.text: Early on the gland is diffusely enlarged and may stay euthyroid because TSH-driven growth compensates. Over years, follicular cells that respond unequally to TSH grow at different rates, and areas of hemorrhage, scarring, and calcification create a multinodular goiter. Some nodules become autonomous and no longer depend on TSH. A large goiter compresses the trachea or esophagus, causing dyspnea or dysphagia, or extends behind the sternum. Iodine deficiency is the most common cause of goiter and hypothyroidism worldwide, while autoimmune thyroiditis is the most common cause where iodine intake is sufficient.

Thyroid hormone enters cells, T4 is converted to T3, and T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors that regulate gene transcription. It raises basal metabolic rate through Na+/K+-ATPase and mitochondrial activity, increases cardiac beta-1 receptors and contractile proteins, increases hepatic LDL receptors, and speeds muscle contraction and relaxation. Hypothyroidism reverses each of these.

blocks.title: Manifestations of hypothyroidism explained by mechanism
rows: Lower basal metabolic rate and heat production
Lower energy expenditure plus fluid and glycosaminoglycan retention
Bradycardia, reduced cardiac output, diastolic hypertension
Fewer beta-1 receptors, weaker contractility, raised peripheral resistance
Myxedema (nonpitting edema, coarse face, large tongue, hoarse voice)
Glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid accumulate in dermis and soft tissue and bind water
Fewer hepatic LDL receptors, so LDL clearance falls
Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
Slower muscle contraction and relaxation from reduced calcium reuptake and myosin ATPase activity
Reduced gut motility, sweat and sebum secretion, and neuronal metabolism
blocks.caption: Each sign reverses a normal action of T3.

blocks.text: TSH is the most sensitive screening test because the pituitary responds to small changes in free T4 with large, roughly logarithmic changes in TSH. That sensitivity depends on a normal pituitary and hypothalamus. Free T4 is read alongside it, because the pairing locates the defect. Typical adult reference ranges are about 0.4 to 4.5 mIU/L for TSH and about 0.8 to 1.8 ng/dL (10 to 23 pmol/L) for free T4, varying by laboratory.

blocks.title: Thyroid function patterns
rows: Gland fails (autoimmune thyroiditis, iodine deficiency, ablation); feedback raises TSH
Early gland failure compensated by TSH
Pituitary or hypothalamus cannot respond; TSH made may also be less bioactive
Autonomous TSH drives the gland despite high T4; often raised glycoprotein alpha subunit
blocks.caption: Discordance, a TSH that fails to move opposite to free T4, signals a pituitary or hypothalamic problem.

blocks.text: Central hypothyroidism is the main trap. A normal TSH looks reassuring, but in the setting of a low free T4 it is inappropriately normal, meaning the pituitary is not responding. Screening with TSH alone therefore misses central disease. A TSH-secreting adenoma is the reverse discordance: both TSH and free T4 are high, and the patient is hyperthyroid with a goiter. The main alternative with the same pattern is thyroid hormone resistance, which is usually familial and lacks a pituitary mass and a raised alpha subunit.

Primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin. Low T4 increases hypothalamic TRH, and TRH stimulates lactotrophs as well as thyrotrophs; clearance of prolactin may also be reduced. Prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH release, so LH and FSH fall, causing anovulation, oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility in women and hypogonadism in men. Prolonged TRH stimulation can also enlarge the pituitary through thyrotroph hyperplasia, which can be mistaken for an adenoma. Restoring thyroid hormone removes the TRH drive, so checking TSH is part of evaluating any hyperprolactinemia.

blocks.title: Worked example: a normal TSH that is not normal
blocks.text: A woman who had a severe postpartum hemorrhage now has fatigue, cold intolerance, and no menses. TSH is 1.2 mIU/L and free T4 is 0.5 ng/dL. Step 1: free T4 is low, so she is hypothyroid. Step 2: with low free T4, the normal pituitary would drive TSH well above range; a TSH of 1.2 is inappropriately normal, so the pituitary is not responding. Step 3: this is central hypothyroidism, and the history points to Sheehan necrosis, so ACTH and gonadotropin deficiency should be expected as well. Had TSH been 25 mIU/L, the defect would be in the thyroid itself.

The thyroid forms from endoderm at the foramen cecum of the tongue and descends along the thyroglossal duct to the front of the neck. The fetal thyroid begins making hormone at about 10 to 12 weeks of gestation. Before then the fetus relies on maternal T4, and some maternal T4 continues to cross the placenta until birth. This explains why most affected newborns look normal at birth. Thyroid hormone is essential for neuronal migration, myelination, and synapse formation in the fetal and early postnatal brain, so untreated deficiency in the first months of life causes permanent intellectual disability.

blocks.title: Causes of congenital hypothyroidism
rows: Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, ectopic gland such as lingual thyroid)
Failure of thyroid formation or descent; most permanent cases where iodine is sufficient
Dyshormonogenesis (thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin, NIS, DUOX2, or pendrin defects)
Inherited, usually autosomal recessive, enzyme or transport defects in hormone synthesis
Yes, because TSH drives a gland that cannot make hormone
Neither mother nor fetus can make enough hormone; most common cause worldwide
Transplacental TSH receptor blocking antibodies or maternal antithyroid drugs
Temporary blockade of the fetal gland
blocks.caption: Goiter at birth points to a synthesis defect or iodine deficiency rather than an absent gland.

blocks.text: The clinical signs reflect slowed metabolism and glycosaminoglycan accumulation, the same mechanisms seen in adults. Infants are lethargic, feed poorly, sleep excessively, and are hypotonic and constipated, with a hoarse cry, dry skin, and a cool body. Jaundice is prolonged and unconjugated, because thyroid hormone is needed for maturation of hepatic bilirubin conjugation. Macroglossia comes from glycosaminoglycan deposition in the tongue, and umbilical hernia from weak abdominal wall tone. A large posterior fontanelle and delayed bone age reflect slowed skeletal maturation. Because symptoms appear late and brain damage starts early, newborn screening detects the disease before it is clinically obvious. Pendred syndrome, a pendrin defect, combines goiter with sensorineural deafness.

The thyroid secretes mostly T4, and most circulating T3 comes from peripheral removal of an outer-ring iodine by type 1 deiodinase (liver, kidney, thyroid) and type 2 deiodinase (brain, pituitary, muscle, brown fat). Type 3 deiodinase removes an inner-ring iodine, converting T4 to inactive reverse T3 (rT3) and T3 to inactive T2. Reverse T3 is itself cleared mainly by type 1 deiodinase.

In severe illness, such as sepsis, myocardial infarction, major surgery, burns, starvation, and critical illness in the intensive care unit, cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha), raised cortisol, and caloric deprivation lower type 1 deiodinase activity and raise type 3 activity. Less T4 becomes T3, more becomes rT3, and rT3 is cleared more slowly, so T3 falls and rT3 rises. This is thought to be an adaptive reduction in catabolism rather than true hypothyroidism. TSH is usually normal or low-normal. In prolonged, severe illness T4 also falls, through reduced binding proteins, circulating binding inhibitors, and central suppression of TRH and TSH by cytokines, glucocorticoids, and dopamine; a low T4 in this setting predicts a worse outcome.

blocks.title: Nonthyroidal illness compared with true hypothyroidism
rows: Usually normal or low-normal; may rise transiently in recovery
Normal, low in severe prolonged illness
blocks.caption: A high reverse T3 favors nonthyroidal illness, because true hypothyroidism supplies less T4 to convert into anything.

blocks.text: Two features cause errors on examinations. During recovery, TSH may rise briefly above normal as the axis restarts, which can be mistaken for primary hypothyroidism. A low T4 with a normal TSH in a critically ill patient can resemble central hypothyroidism; the raised rT3 and the clinical setting point to illness instead.

Short stature is usually defined as height more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex. Growth velocity, bone age, and parental heights matter more than a single measurement. GH is secreted in pulses, mainly during sleep, under stimulation by GHRH and ghrelin and inhibition by somatostatin. It binds the GH receptor, which signals through JAK2 and STAT5b, mainly in the liver, to produce IGF-1. IGF-1 drives chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plates and feeds back to suppress GH. Because GH secretion is pulsatile, a single GH level is uninformative, while IGF-1 reflects average GH activity.

blocks.title: Distinguishing causes of short stature
rows: Slow growth velocity; increased fat, chubby appearance; neonatal hypoglycemia possible
Severe growth failure; GH high because IGF-1 feedback is lost
Normal or low for age, normal for bone age
Normal velocity, late puberty, often a parent who matured late; reaches normal adult height
Normal velocity and puberty timing; adult height short but in line with parental heights
Slow growth with weight relatively preserved
blocks.caption: Bone age separates familial short stature (normal) from the delayed forms; GH and IGF-1 separate GH deficiency from receptor resistance.

blocks.text: The key distinction is between a child who grows slowly and one who grows at a normal rate along a low percentile. Endocrine causes reduce growth velocity and delay bone age, and weight is usually relatively preserved, so the child looks heavy for height. Malnutrition and chronic disease such as celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease usually reduce weight first. Bone age shows how much growth remains: when it lags behind chronological age, the growth plates stay open longer and catch-up growth is possible, as in constitutional delay. When bone age matches chronological age, the child is simply following a genetically short trajectory.

Laron syndrome is end-organ resistance, the growth equivalent of pseudohypoparathyroidism: the hormone is high because the receptor cannot respond and the feedback signal (IGF-1) is missing. Other causes include Turner syndrome in girls, glucocorticoid excess (growth failure with weight gain), and skeletal dysplasias, which produce disproportionate short stature.

integration.text: Across this chapter, three principles from physiology predict the pathology. First, feedback loops locate the lesion: high ACTH, TSH, or PTH with a low target effect means the gland or end organ has failed, and a low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone means the pituitary or hypothalamus has failed. End-organ resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, pseudohypoparathyroidism, Laron syndrome) produces a deficiency picture with high hormone levels. Second, each missing hormone explains its own signs through the kidney, vessel, nerve, or cell it normally acts on: aldosterone through principal cells, cortisol through vascular tone and free water excretion, PTH through nephron calcium and phosphate handling, and T3 through nuclear receptors. Third, anatomy and embryology predict which glands fail together: the stalk links ADH, dopamine, and releasing hormones; the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches link the parathyroids and thymus; and autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes link the adrenal, parathyroid, and thyroid.

Immunology and microbiology supply the most common causes: autoimmunity in developed countries, tuberculosis and iodine deficiency worldwide, and meningococcal sepsis for adrenal hemorrhage. The limits are worth knowing. Laboratory cutoffs differ between assays and references, a single hormone value can mislead when pulsatile secretion, binding proteins, or acute illness alter it, and several deficiencies can mask one another, as when ACTH deficiency hides diabetes insipidus.

summary: Pair each trophic hormone with its target hormone: high trophic with low target means primary failure; low or inappropriately normal trophic means pituitary or hypothalamic failure.

Central diabetes insipidus lacks ADH; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus cannot respond to it (V2 receptor, aquaporin-2, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia); both give dilute polyuria, with hypernatremia only when water intake is limited.
On water deprivation, primary polydipsia concentrates urine, central diabetes insipidus concentrates only after desmopressin, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus does not concentrate at all.
Addison disease removes cortisol and aldosterone: hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and hyperpigmentation from high ACTH and POMC-derived peptides.
Adrenal crisis is cortisol deficiency under stress, steroid withdrawal, or bilateral hemorrhage; loss of cortisol's permissive effect on vascular tone produces shock resistant to fluids and pressors.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low ACTH, so there is no hyperpigmentation, and angiotensin II preserves aldosterone, so there is no hyperkalemia.
Hypoparathyroidism gives low calcium, high phosphate, and low PTH; low calcium lowers the nerve firing threshold (tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs) and prolongs phase 2 and the QT interval.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a is maternally inherited GNAS loss with high PTH and Albright hereditary osteodystrophy; paternal inheritance gives the phenotype without hypocalcemia.
Hypothalamic and stalk lesions lower anterior pituitary hormones, cause diabetes insipidus, and raise prolactin by cutting off dopamine; primary empty sella usually leaves pituitary function intact.

Iodine deficiency raises TSH and causes diffuse then multinodular goiter; euthyroid sick syndrome has low T3, high reverse T3, and usually normal TSH; bone age separates familial short stature from delayed growth.

verify: Water deprivation test cutoffs (stopping criteria, the percentage rise after desmopressin that separates complete and partial central diabetes insipidus from nephrogenic disease) vary between protocols; confirm the values NABNE expects. Copeptin-based testing is not covered.
The fraction of gland destroyed before symptoms appear (about 90% for the adrenal cortex, about 75% for the anterior pituitary) is quoted differently across sources.
The dose and duration of exogenous glucocorticoid that suppresses the HPA axis are not stated here because thresholds vary by source; confirm whether NABNE tests a specific figure.
The usual order of hormone loss in gradual hypopituitarism (GH and gonadotropins, then TSH, then ACTH) is a teaching generalization with exceptions, such as early prolactin loss in Sheehan necrosis.
The prolactin level typical of the stalk effect is given only as mildly raised; confirm whether NABNE uses a numeric cutoff.
Reference ranges for TSH, free T4, calcium, phosphate, and sodium vary by laboratory; values given are approximate adult ranges.
Iodine requirement (about 150 micrograms per day in adults) follows WHO and US guidance; pregnancy requirements are quoted as about 220 to 250 micrograms per day.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Chvostek, Trousseau, Albright, Laron, Sheehan, Waterhouse-Friderichsen, and Pendred, or only descriptive terms.
